stimuli.title: The bank at the village shop
stimuli.content:
In many Indian villages, the nearest bank branch is still several kilometres away, and a trip to it can cost a farmer or a daily-wage worker a full day's earnings. To bridge this gap, banks appoint business correspondents: local shopkeepers, retired teachers or members of self-help groups who are trained to offer basic banking services from their own premises. Equipped with a biometric device and a small terminal, a correspondent can open a savings account, accept deposits, pay out small withdrawals and help villagers receive government benefits directly in their accounts.

The model has clear advantages. Because the correspondent is a familiar face, people who once felt nervous about entering a bank are more willing to save. Transactions happen close to home and at hours that suit working people, often in the evening after work in the fields is over. For the bank, the cost of serving a customer through a correspondent is a fraction of the cost of running a full branch.

The arrangement is not without problems, however. Correspondents earn a commission on each transaction, and in areas where transactions are few and small, the income may not be enough to keep them interested. Network failures can leave a customer waiting for hours, and when the cash at the counter runs short, withdrawals are delayed. Some customers also complain that they do not receive a printed receipt and therefore cannot check whether their money has been recorded correctly.

Experts argue that the solution lies in better pay for correspondents, reliable connectivity and simple ways for customers to verify every transaction on their phones. If these gaps are filled, the village shop may become as trusted as the bank itself.

stimuli.title: Saving the rain
stimuli.content:
Every monsoon, many Indian cities face a strange contradiction. Streets flood after a few hours of heavy rain, yet a few months later the same neighbourhoods queue up for water tankers. The reason is simple: most of the rain that falls on roofs, roads and paved courtyards runs straight into drains and is lost, while the groundwater that residents depend on in summer keeps falling year after year.

Rainwater harvesting offers a low-cost way out of this cycle. In its simplest form, water from a rooftop is led through pipes into a filter and then into a storage tank or a recharge pit. Water stored in a tank can be used for washing and gardening, while water sent into a recharge pit seeps into the ground and gradually raises the water table. A house with a roof of a hundred square metres in a city that receives moderate rainfall can capture tens of thousands of litres in a single season.

Several city governments have made rainwater harvesting compulsory for new buildings, but enforcement has been uneven. In many cases, structures are built only to obtain an approval certificate and are never cleaned or maintained afterwards. A recharge pit clogged with silt does little more than collect mosquitoes.

The lesson from places where the practice has worked is that rules alone are not enough. Where resident associations take charge of maintenance, and where people can see the water level in their own borewells rising, harvesting becomes a habit rather than a formality. Public awareness, in short, matters as much as public regulation.

stimuli.title: The weakest link in digital payments
stimuli.content:
Over the past decade, the technology behind digital payments has become remarkably secure. Transactions are encrypted, devices are bound to specific phone numbers, and a payment cannot usually be completed without a PIN or a one-time password known only to the customer. Ironically, it is this very strength that has shifted the attention of fraudsters away from the system and towards its users. Rather than break the code, they persuade the customer to open the door.

The methods are varied but follow a common script. A caller claims to be from the bank's 'security team' and warns that the customer's account will be frozen unless a document is updated immediately. A message offers a refund for a failed delivery, and a link leads to a page that looks exactly like the customer's banking app. In each case, the victim is rushed, frightened or flattered into sharing a code or approving a request that moves money out of the account. Because the customer has technically authorised the payment, recovering the money is often difficult.

Banks have responded with warnings printed on statements, pop-up alerts in apps and cooling-off periods for new payees. Some have begun to use software that flags unusual behaviour, such as a large transfer to a new beneficiary minutes after a long phone call. These measures help, but they cannot entirely replace the judgement of the customer. A warning that appears on every screen soon becomes invisible.

The more durable defence may be cultural rather than technical. Just as people learned over generations not to hand over their house keys to a stranger at the door, they will need to learn that no genuine bank official will ever ask for a PIN. Until that instinct becomes second nature, the security of the system will be only as strong as the caution of its least careful user.

stimuli.title: Work without a workplace
stimuli.content:
A delivery rider in a large Indian city may work for three platforms in a single day, switching apps depending on which offers the better rate at that hour. He has no manager he has ever met, no fixed hours and no office. To the platforms, he is not an employee but a 'partner', an independent contractor who chooses when and how much to work. To many economists, he represents one of the fastest-growing segments of the urban labour force.

The flexibility of gig work is real, and many workers value it. Students fit deliveries around classes; homemakers drive cabs during school hours; people between jobs earn an income while they search. For workers with few formal qualifications, platforms have lowered the barriers to entry that once kept them out of steady earnings.

But flexibility has a cost that is easy to overlook in good times. A gig worker who falls ill earns nothing until he recovers. He has no provident fund, no gratuity and, in most cases, no health insurance beyond what he buys himself. Because his income is spread across several platforms, none of them considers itself responsible for his welfare. An accident on the road can wipe out months of savings.

Recent labour codes have, for the first time, recognised gig and platform workers as a distinct category and provided for social security schemes funded partly by contributions from aggregators. The idea is sound, but its success will depend on details that are still being worked out: how contributions are calculated when a worker serves several platforms, how benefits travel with him when he switches apps, and how a worker with no employer proves his eligibility. A safety net, after all, is useful only if those who fall can actually land in it.

stimuli.title: The colour of money
stimuli.content:
Few labels have spread through financial markets as quickly as 'green'. Bonds that fund solar parks, loans linked to emission targets and funds that screen out polluting companies have multiplied, and banks now compete to announce ever larger commitments to sustainable finance. For a planet that needs vast sums to decarbonise, the enthusiasm is welcome. The difficulty is that enthusiasm is cheaper than accountability.

A label is only as meaningful as the standard behind it, and for years the standards were largely written by those who used them. A company could issue a 'sustainability-linked' bond whose targets it was already on course to meet, or a fund could call itself green while holding the shares of firms whose principal business was extracting coal, provided those firms had published a transition plan. None of this was necessarily dishonest; much of it was simply vague. But vagueness has a way of favouring the issuer over the investor, and a market in which every product can claim virtue soon becomes one in which none can be trusted.

Regulators have begun to respond with taxonomies that define which activities qualify as sustainable and disclosure rules that require firms to back their claims with data. Critics complain that these rules add paperwork, and that a rigid definition may exclude genuinely useful projects that do not fit neatly into any category. The objection is not frivolous. A cement plant that halves its emissions does more for the climate than a solar firm that merely exists, yet only the latter may qualify for the label.

The answer is unlikely to lie in abandoning standards, but in making them measure change rather than identity. Investors should ask not whether a firm looks green today but whether it is becoming less brown, and at what pace. Money, after all, has no colour; it is what money does that the label ought to describe.

stimuli.title: A dividend that must be earned
stimuli.content:
Demographers speak of a 'dividend' when a country's working-age population grows faster than the number of children and elderly people who depend on it. With more earners for every dependant, savings rise, investment becomes easier to finance and growth can accelerate. Several East Asian economies rode such a wave in the late twentieth century, and India, with a median age still below thirty, is often said to be riding one now.

The metaphor, however, is misleading in one important respect. A dividend is something a shareholder receives simply for owning a share; it requires no further effort. The demographic dividend is nothing of the kind. A large cohort of young people becomes an asset only if they are healthy, educated and absorbed into productive work. If they are not, the same cohort becomes a burden: a generation of under-employed adults who save little, pay little tax and grow old without the savings to support themselves.

The East Asian economies that benefited did not merely possess young populations; they invested heavily in schooling, moved workers out of low-productivity farming into manufacturing, and drew women into the paid workforce in large numbers. The last point is often neglected. A country in which a large share of working-age women do not participate in paid work is, in effect, collecting only part of its dividend, however favourable its age structure may appear.

The window does not stay open indefinitely. As fertility falls, the working-age share eventually peaks and begins to decline, and the country must then support a growing elderly population. A nation that has not grown rich by then may find that it has grown old first. The question for policymakers, therefore, is not whether the dividend exists but whether the conditions to collect it are being created quickly enough.

stimuli.title: Learning to save early
stimuli.content:
Financial habits, like most habits, are formed early. A child who receives a small allowance and is encouraged to keep part of it aside learns a lesson that no textbook can (1) ______: that money spent today is money that cannot be spent tomorrow. Unfortunately, many young adults enter their first job without ever having (2) ______ a budget, and the arrival of a regular salary, together with easy access to credit cards and instant loans, can quickly lead to debt.

Schools and banks can play a useful role here. Several banks now run programmes in which students open a savings account, (3) ______ small amounts every month and track how interest makes their balance grow. Such exercises turn an abstract idea into something the student can see and measure. Teachers report that students who take part are more (4) ______ about comparing prices and less likely to buy things on impulse.

Parents, too, have a part to play. Children learn more from what they see than from what they are told, and a household in which expenses are discussed openly gives them a realistic picture of how money is earned and used. Talking about money need not be (5) ______; it can be as ordinary as discussing the weather.

The aim is not to make children anxious about money but to make them confident with it. A young person who understands saving, borrowing and interest is far better (6) ______ to make the large financial decisions that adult life brings.

stimuli.title: The second life of batteries
stimuli.content:
As electric vehicles move from novelty to the mainstream, a question that once seemed distant is becoming urgent: what happens to their batteries when they wear out? A typical vehicle battery is considered unfit for driving once its capacity falls to about seventy or eighty per cent of the original, but that does not mean it is (1) ______. Such a battery can still store a great deal of energy, and a growing number of firms are giving it a second life as stationary storage for solar panels, telecom towers and small shops.

When even this second life ends, the battery must be recycled. Lithium, cobalt and nickel are expensive to mine and are concentrated in a handful of countries, so recovering them from old cells reduces both costs and (2) ______ on imports. Recycling, however, is technically demanding. Batteries differ widely in design, and dismantling them safely requires skilled labour and careful handling of materials that can catch fire.

At present, a large share of used batteries in many developing countries passes through informal dealers who extract the most valuable parts and (3) ______ the rest, often in ways that pollute soil and water. Bringing these dealers into the formal system, rather than simply banning them, may be the most practical way forward.

Policy can help by making manufacturers responsible for collecting the batteries they sell and by setting minimum recovery targets. If the rules are clear and enforced, the battery that leaves a car may become not a waste problem but a (4) ______ of raw material for the next generation of vehicles.

stimuli.title: When credit becomes a trap
stimuli.content:
Microfinance began with a simple and powerful insight: poor households, especially women, are reliable borrowers when loans are small, repayments are frequent and borrowers in a group (1) ______ for one another. For two decades, the model brought formal credit to millions who had previously depended on moneylenders charging ruinous rates.

Success, however, brought its own risks. As lenders multiplied and competed for the same customers, some borrowers took loans from several institutions at once, using one loan to repay another. Because no single lender could see the full picture, a household's total debt could grow well beyond what its income could (2) ______. When a crop failed or a family member fell ill, repayments stopped, and the stress spread quickly through entire villages. Some families sold their livestock, and others went back to the very moneylenders that microfinance had been meant to replace.

The lesson was not that small loans are harmful but that lending without information is. Credit bureaus now record microfinance loans, and regulators have introduced limits linking a household's total repayment obligations to its income. These rules aim to (3) ______ the kind of over-lending that had turned a tool of empowerment into a source of distress.

Yet rules can only do so much. Responsible lending also depends on loan officers who are judged by the quality of the loans they make, not merely by how many they disburse. An institution that rewards its staff only for volume will always find ways around a ceiling. In finance, as elsewhere, incentives tend to (4) ______ intentions.

stimuli.title: Cities that cool themselves
stimuli.content:
On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees hotter than the farmland around it. This 'urban heat island' is no mystery. Concrete and asphalt absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night, while the trees and open soil that would otherwise **(1) aggravate** the heat have been paved over. Air conditioners, which pump hot air out of buildings and into the streets, make the problem **(2) better**.

The consequences are not merely uncomfortable. Prolonged heat raises the risk of illness among the elderly and outdoor workers, **(3) elevates** labour productivity and pushes up demand for electricity at the very hours when grids are most strained. In a warming climate, heat is fast becoming one of the most serious, if least **(4) visible**, threats to urban life.

Fortunately, many of the remedies are simple. Roofs painted in reflective white can lower indoor temperatures noticeably; trees planted along streets provide shade and cool the air through evaporation; and water bodies that were filled in for construction can be restored. Some cities have drawn up 'heat action plans' that combine such measures with early warnings and changes in working hours during heatwaves.

What these plans require is not exotic technology but **(5) occasional** attention. A tree planted this year will cast useful shade only after several years of care, and a white roof must be repainted as it fades. Cooling a city, in other words, is less a single project than a habit of maintenance.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a service offered by a business correspondent?

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: The first paragraph lists the correspondent's services: opening savings accounts, accepting deposits, paying small withdrawals and helping villagers receive government benefits. Sanctioning crop loans is never mentioned.
steps: Locate the list of services in paragraph 1
Tick off the options found there: account opening, deposits, government benefits
Crop loans do not appear anywhere in the passage, so C is the answer
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and D are all named in the first paragraph as services a correspondent provides, so they cannot be the 'NOT mentioned' answer.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, are villagers more willing to save through a business correspondent?

options.text: Correspondents pay a higher rate of interest than bank branches.
The correspondent is a familiar person, which reduces their nervousness.
Government benefits can be received only through correspondents.
Correspondents do not charge the bank any commission.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that because the correspondent is a familiar face, people who once felt nervous about entering a bank are more willing to save.
steps: Find the sentence about willingness to save: paragraph 2, sentence 2
The reason given is familiarity, which removes nervousness
solution.why_others_wrong: A: interest rates are never compared. C: the passage says correspondents help people receive benefits, not that this is the only channel. D: the passage says correspondents earn a commission on each transaction.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The correspondent is a familiar person, which reduces their nervousness.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following problems with the correspondent model is/are mentioned in the passage?
(i) Low commission income in areas with few transactions
(ii) Delays caused by network failures
(iii) Correspondents refusing to serve elderly customers

solution.concept: Checking each statement against the passage
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 mentions low commission income where transactions are few and small, and network failures that leave customers waiting. Nothing is said about correspondents refusing elderly customers.
steps: (i): 'the income may not be enough to keep them interested': mentioned
(ii): 'Network failures can leave a customer waiting for hours': mentioned
solution.why_others_wrong: A leaves out (i), which is clearly stated. B and C include (iii), which the passage never mentions.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is most similar in meaning to the word 'bridge' as used in the passage ('To bridge this gap')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: 'bridge a gap' means to reduce or close a gap
solution.explanation: Banks appoint correspondents to remove the distance between villagers and banking services. To 'bridge a gap' is to close it, so 'close' fits.
steps: Read the sentence: the gap is the distance between villages and bank branches
Correspondents are appointed to remove that distance
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Ignore' and 'widen' are opposite to what the correspondents are meant to do. 'Measure' does not remove the gap at all.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the author's view of the business correspondent model?

options.text: It has failed and should be replaced by more bank branches.
It is perfect and needs no change.
It is useful, but its shortcomings must be fixed for it to succeed fully.
It benefits banks but offers nothing to villagers.

solution.concept: Author's overall view: weigh the advantages against the problems the passage lists
solution.explanation: The author lists clear advantages (paragraph 2), then real problems (paragraph 3), and ends by saying that if these gaps are filled the village shop may become as trusted as the bank. That is a balanced, positive-but-conditional view.
steps: Paragraph 2: advantages for villagers and banks
Paragraph 4: solutions, with a hopeful conclusion
So the model is useful but needs fixing: C
solution.why_others_wrong: A: the author never says the model failed or calls for more branches. B: paragraph 3 lists problems. D: paragraph 2 lists clear benefits to villagers.
solution.final_answer: Option C: It is useful, but its shortcomings must be fixed for it to succeed fully.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what happens to most of the rain that falls on roofs, roads and paved courtyards in cities?

options.text: It is stored in public tanks.
It evaporates before it reaches the ground.
It runs into drains and is lost.

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: The first paragraph says most of this rain 'runs straight into drains and is lost'.
steps: Find the sentence beginning 'The reason is simple' in paragraph 1
It says the rain runs into drains and is lost
solution.why_others_wrong: A and B describe what harvesting could achieve, not what happens now; the passage says groundwater keeps falling. C (evaporation) is not mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option D: It runs into drains and is lost.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, water collected in a storage tank can be used for

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says water stored in a tank 'can be used for washing and gardening'.
steps: Find the sentence about the storage tank in paragraph 2
solution.why_others_wrong: Drinking without treatment, industrial cooling and supplying tankers are not mentioned as uses of stored water.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What can be inferred about harvesting structures that are built 'only to obtain an approval certificate'?

options.text: They usually capture more water than is required.
They are maintained by resident associations.
They are often neglected and so stop working effectively.
They are exempt from the city's rules.

solution.concept: Inference from the surrounding sentences
solution.explanation: The passage says such structures 'are never cleaned or maintained afterwards' and that a pit clogged with silt 'does little more than collect mosquitoes'. So they are neglected and become ineffective.
steps: Read the sentence and the one after it in paragraph 3
Never cleaned or maintained + clogged pit collects mosquitoes = neglect leads to failure
solution.why_others_wrong: A has no support. B is the opposite: resident associations appear in paragraph 4 as the remedy. D contradicts the passage, since the certificate is obtained precisely to satisfy the rules.
solution.final_answer: Option C: They are often neglected and so stop working effectively.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: Harvesting the Rain: Why Rules Need Public Participation

solution.concept: A title must cover the whole passage, not one detail
solution.explanation: The passage introduces the problem, explains rainwater harvesting, shows that compulsory rules have been poorly enforced and concludes that public involvement matters as much as regulation. Option B covers all of this.
steps: Para 1: the problem; para 2: the solution; para 3: weak enforcement; para 4: people must take part
The title must mention harvesting and the role of the public
solution.why_others_wrong: A covers only the first paragraph. C focuses on one technical detail. D picks up a passing reference to tankers.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Harvesting the Rain: Why Rules Need Public Participation

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why have fraudsters shifted their attention from the payment system to its users?

options.text: The technology has become so secure that deceiving users is easier than breaking it.
Users are legally responsible for every failed transaction.
Banks have stopped using one-time passwords.
Encryption prevents users from reporting fraud.

solution.concept: Cause and effect stated in the passage
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 says it is 'this very strength' of the technology that shifted fraudsters' attention to users: 'Rather than break the code, they persuade the customer to open the door.'
steps: Locate 'Ironically, it is this very strength...' in paragraph 1
'This very strength' = the security of the technology
So fraudsters find it easier to deceive users than to break the system: option A
solution.why_others_wrong: B: legal responsibility for failed transactions is not discussed. C contradicts the passage, which says payments usually need a PIN or OTP. D: encryption is mentioned only as a security feature.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The technology has become so secure that deceiving users is easier than breaking it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why is it often difficult to recover money lost in such frauds?

options.text: The fraudsters usually operate from other countries.
The customer has technically authorised the payment.
Banks do not keep records of such transactions.
The money is always withdrawn as cash immediately.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 2 says: 'Because the customer has technically authorised the payment, recovering the money is often difficult.'
steps: The reason given is that the customer technically authorised it
solution.why_others_wrong: A, C and D introduce reasons the passage never mentions.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The customer has technically authorised the payment.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author mean by the statement 'A warning that appears on every screen soon becomes invisible'?

options.text: Warnings are printed in a font too small to read.
Banks withdraw warnings after a short period.
Fraudsters hide warnings using malicious software.
Users stop noticing warnings that are repeated too often.

solution.concept: Interpreting a figurative statement
solution.explanation: The warning does not literally disappear; seeing it everywhere makes users stop paying attention to it. That is why, the author says, banks' measures cannot replace the customer's own judgement.
steps: Repetition leads to users ignoring it: option D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C read 'invisible' literally and add details (font size, withdrawal of warnings, malware) that the passage does not mention.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Users stop noticing warnings that are repeated too often.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.text: Software that flags unusual behaviour has eliminated payment fraud.
Most digital payments today can be made without a PIN.
The author believes customer awareness is at least as important as technical safeguards.
Banks have been unwilling to warn customers about fraud.

solution.concept: Inference consistent with the whole passage
solution.explanation: The author says banks' measures 'help, but they cannot entirely replace the judgement of the customer', and calls the cultural defence 'more durable'. So the author values customer awareness at least as much as technical safeguards.
steps: Paragraph 3: technical measures help but cannot replace judgement
Paragraph 4: the more durable defence is cultural
Option C follows; check that the others contradict the passage
solution.why_others_wrong: A: the passage says such measures 'help', not that they eliminate fraud. B contradicts paragraph 1. D contradicts paragraph 3, which lists the warnings banks give.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The author believes customer awareness is at least as important as technical safeguards.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to the word 'durable' as used in the passage?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: 'durable' means long-lasting
solution.explanation: 'The more durable defence' is a defence that lasts longer. The opposite is 'short-lived'.
steps: Meaning of 'durable' in the sentence: lasting, able to hold over time
Look for the option that means 'not lasting'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Permanent', 'robust' and 'enduring' are all close in meaning to 'durable', not opposite.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The tone of the passage is best described as

solution.concept: Identifying tone from word choice and structure
solution.explanation: The author explains why fraud has shifted to users, examines the banks' responses and warns readers that security depends on the caution of users. That is analytical and cautionary.
steps: The passage explains causes and evaluates measures: analytical
It ends with a warning about the 'least careful user': cautionary
No blame, panic, indifference or celebration
solution.why_others_wrong: A: the author blames neither banks nor customers and does not exaggerate. C: the author is clearly concerned. D: the passage praises the technology only to explain the shift of fraud to users.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT cited in the passage as an example of how people use the flexibility of gig work?

options.text: Students fitting deliveries around their classes
Homemakers driving cabs during school hours
People earning an income while they look for a job

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives three examples: students, homemakers and people between jobs. Retired employees are not mentioned.
steps: Match A, B and C to the three examples
Retired employees do not appear: option D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are the three examples listed in paragraph 2, so they cannot be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Retired employees supplementing their pensions

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, does no single platform consider itself responsible for a gig worker's welfare?

options.text: The worker's income is spread across several platforms.
Platforms are not registered in India.
Gig workers refuse to sign contracts with platforms.
The law forbids platforms from offering insurance.

solution.concept: Cause stated in the passage
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 says: 'Because his income is spread across several platforms, none of them considers itself responsible for his welfare.'
steps: Locate 'responsible for his welfare' in paragraph 3
The reason is the spread of income across platforms
solution.why_others_wrong: B, C and D introduce facts the passage never states; D also contradicts paragraph 4, where aggregators are asked to contribute to social security.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The worker's income is spread across several platforms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The phrase 'a cost that is easy to overlook in good times' suggests that

options.text: gig work becomes more expensive for customers during festivals
the lack of protection becomes apparent only when the worker falls ill or meets with an accident
platforms raise their commissions when demand is high
workers save too much money when their income is high

solution.concept: Inference from the sentences that follow a claim
solution.explanation: The sentences after the phrase describe illness, no provident fund or insurance, and accidents wiping out savings. The 'cost' of flexibility is the absence of protection, which shows only when something goes wrong.
steps: 'Good times' = when the worker is healthy and earning
The examples that follow are illness and accidents
So the cost is hidden until misfortune strikes: option B
solution.why_others_wrong: A and C talk about prices and commissions, which the passage does not discuss. D reverses the point: the passage says an accident can wipe out savings.
solution.final_answer: Option B: the lack of protection becomes apparent only when the worker falls ill or meets with an accident

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, which of the following aspects of the new social security provisions is still being worked out?

options.text: Whether gig workers should be recognised as a separate category
Whether aggregators should contribute at all
How contributions are to be calculated for a worker who serves several platforms
Whether students should be allowed to take up gig work

solution.concept: Locating a detail in a list
solution.explanation: The last paragraph lists three unresolved details: calculating contributions for a worker serving several platforms, carrying benefits across apps and proving eligibility without an employer.
steps: Find 'details that are still being worked out' in paragraph 4
The first detail listed is how contributions are calculated across platforms
solution.why_others_wrong: A and B are already settled: the codes have recognised gig workers and provided for aggregator contributions. D is not discussed.
solution.final_answer: Option C: How contributions are to be calculated for a worker who serves several platforms

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is most similar in meaning to the word 'distinct' as used in the passage ('as a distinct category')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context
solution.explanation: The labour codes recognised gig workers as a category of their own, different from employees. 'Distinct' here means separate.
steps: Context: gig workers were recognised 'for the first time' as their own category
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Vague' is nearly the opposite of 'distinct'. 'Famous' and 'temporary' do not fit the meaning of a legal category.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Gig work offers real flexibility, but workers need a social safety net that actually works for them.
Gig work should be banned because it offers no security.
Platforms are the main cause of unemployment in cities.
Recent labour codes have fully solved the problems of gig workers.

solution.concept: Central idea: balance all paragraphs
solution.explanation: The passage grants that flexibility is real and valued, describes the missing protections and welcomes the new codes while warning that the details must work. Option A captures this balance.
steps: Para 2: flexibility is valuable; para 3: protections are missing
Para 4: new codes are sound, but details decide success
solution.why_others_wrong: B is too extreme; the author values flexibility. C is never claimed. D contradicts paragraph 4, which says the details are still being worked out.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Gig work offers real flexibility, but workers need a social safety net that actually works for them.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The statement 'enthusiasm is cheaper than accountability' most nearly implies that

options.text: green projects cost less to build than conventional projects
it is easier to announce sustainable commitments than to be held answerable for meeting them
investors are unwilling to pay for independent audits
regulators charge high fees for green certification

solution.concept: Interpreting a figurative claim in context
solution.explanation: The sentence follows the description of banks competing to announce ever larger commitments. 'Cheaper' is figurative: announcing is easy, while being held to account for results is costly and demanding. The next paragraph develops exactly this gap between labels and standards.
steps: So announcing is easier than delivering: option B
solution.why_others_wrong: A reads 'cheaper' literally as project cost. C and D bring in audits and certification fees, which the passage never mentions.
solution.final_answer: Option B: it is easier to announce sustainable commitments than to be held answerable for meeting them

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following can be inferred about the early standards for green finance described in the second paragraph?

options.text: Since they were framed largely by the issuers themselves, they tended to be loose in ways that favoured issuers.
They were mostly drafted by independent climate scientists.
They were deliberately designed to defraud investors.
They excluded all coal-related companies from green funds.

solution.concept: Inference that stays within the author's claims
solution.explanation: The standards were 'largely written by those who used them', allowed easy targets and coal holdings, and were 'simply vague'; vagueness 'has a way of favouring the issuer over the investor'. Option A combines these points.
steps: Who wrote the standards? Those who used them (issuers)
What were they like? Vague, permissive
Whom did vagueness favour? The issuer
So A; check that C overstates and D contradicts
solution.why_others_wrong: B contradicts 'written by those who used them'. C overstates: the author says 'None of this was necessarily dishonest'. D contradicts the example of a green fund holding coal firms.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Since they were framed largely by the issuers themselves, they tended to be loose in ways that favoured issuers.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The author uses the example of the cement plant and the solar firm mainly to show that

options.text: cement production is more harmful to the climate than solar power
solar firms should not receive green finance at all
regulators favour heavy industry over renewable energy
a definition based on the type of activity may reward identity rather than an actual cut in emissions

solution.concept: Purpose of an example
solution.explanation: The example comes right after the critics' point that rigid definitions can exclude useful projects. A cement plant halving its emissions helps the climate more, yet only the solar firm 'may qualify for the label'. The author's conclusion that standards should 'measure change rather than identity' confirms the purpose.
steps: Locate the example: paragraph 3, after 'The objection is not frivolous'
Contrast: real emission cut (cement) vs merely being a solar firm
Link to paragraph 4: 'measure change rather than identity'
solution.why_others_wrong: A is a factual comparison the example does not aim at. B goes too far; the author does not oppose financing solar firms. C reverses the point: under current definitions, the solar firm qualifies and the cement plant may not.
solution.final_answer: Option D: a definition based on the type of activity may reward identity rather than an actual cut in emissions

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The author's attitude towards the critics of the new regulations can best be described as

solution.concept: Tone towards a viewpoint: look for concessions and limits
solution.explanation: The author concedes 'The objection is not frivolous' and gives an example supporting it, but then says the answer is not to abandon standards but to redesign them. That is partial agreement: partly sympathetic.
steps: Concession: 'The objection is not frivolous' plus a supporting example
Limit: 'The answer is unlikely to lie in abandoning standards'
solution.why_others_wrong: A and B are ruled out by the explicit concession. D overstates: the author does not accept the critics' complaint about paperwork and keeps the case for standards.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The word 'frivolous' as used in the passage ('The objection is not frivolous') is closest in meaning to

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: frivolous = lacking serious purpose or value
solution.explanation: 'Not frivolous' means the objection deserves to be taken seriously. So 'frivolous' itself means trivial.
steps: The author supports the objection with an example, so 'not frivolous' = worth taking seriously
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Serious' is the opposite of 'frivolous'; it is the meaning of 'not frivolous'. 'Dishonest' and 'complex' are unrelated in meaning.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the author, the term 'dividend' is misleading because

options.text: India's working-age population has already begun to shrink
dividends are usually paid only to elderly shareholders
unlike a financial dividend, the demographic benefit does not come automatically but depends on deliberate investment
East Asian economies gained nothing from their young populations

solution.concept: Understanding an argument about a metaphor
solution.explanation: A shareholder's dividend 'requires no further effort', but a young population becomes an asset 'only if they are healthy, educated and absorbed into productive work'. The benefit has to be earned through investment.
steps: Financial dividend: no effort needed; demographic dividend: needs health, education and jobs
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts paragraph 1 (India is said to be riding the wave now). B is a distortion of what a dividend is. D contradicts paragraph 3, which says the East Asian economies benefited.
solution.final_answer: Option C: unlike a financial dividend, the demographic benefit does not come automatically but depends on deliberate investment

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following statements would the author most likely agree with?

options.text: A young population by itself guarantees rapid economic growth.
Countries should try to raise fertility so that the demographic window stays open.
Investment in schooling matters less than the size of the working-age population.
Low participation of women in paid work reduces the benefit a country can draw from a favourable age structure.

solution.concept: Agree/disagree inference
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a country where many working-age women do not do paid work is 'collecting only part of its dividend, however favourable its age structure may appear'. That is option D.
steps: Test each option against the passage
A contradicts the central claim that the dividend must be earned
B: the author never proposes raising fertility
C reverses paragraph 3, which stresses schooling
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are each contradicted by, or absent from, the passage, as shown in the steps.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Low participation of women in paid work reduces the benefit a country can draw from a favourable age structure.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The phrase 'may find that it has grown old first' suggests that

options.text: the country's elderly population may become large before the country is prosperous enough to support it
the country will age faster than every other country in the world
older citizens will be forced to keep working after retirement
the demographic window will reopen once the population ages

solution.concept: Interpreting a phrase from its sentence
solution.explanation: The full sentence is 'A nation that has not grown rich by then may find that it has grown old first'. 'First' means before growing rich: ageing arrives before prosperity.
steps: Read the whole sentence: 'not grown rich by then ... grown old first'
So the elderly burden arrives before the wealth to bear it: option A
solution.why_others_wrong: B makes an unsupported comparison with all countries. C is not mentioned. D contradicts 'The window does not stay open indefinitely'.
solution.final_answer: Option A: the country's elderly population may become large before the country is prosperous enough to support it

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following titles best captures the main argument of the passage?

options.text: The Demographic Dividend: An Opportunity, Not an Entitlement

solution.concept: Title = main argument, not a supporting detail
solution.explanation: The author's main argument is that a young population is a benefit only if a country creates the conditions to collect it, and must do so before the window closes. 'An Opportunity, Not an Entitlement' expresses that.
steps: Main claim (para 2): the dividend must be earned
Support (para 3): East Asia earned it; women's participation matters
solution.why_others_wrong: A: the passage says India is young now; ageing is a future risk. C is one supporting example. D: the causes of falling fertility are not discussed.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The Demographic Dividend: An Opportunity, Not an Entitlement

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: meaning of the sentence decides the word
solution.explanation: The child 'learns a lesson that no textbook can teach': a textbook is something that teaches, so 'teach' completes the idea that this lesson is learned from experience.
steps: What does a textbook do with a lesson? It teaches it
solution.why_others_wrong: A textbook cannot 'learn', 'forget' or 'borrow' a lesson; these verbs do not suit a book as subject.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: collocation ('prepare a budget')
solution.explanation: Young adults start work 'without ever having prepared a budget', which explains why a salary and easy credit lead them into debt. 'Prepare a budget' is the standard collocation.
steps: The sentence explains why young earners fall into debt
They lack practice in planning money
solution.why_others_wrong: One does not 'earn', 'borrow' or 'refuse' a budget in this sense; none of these explains the slide into debt.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: logical sequence of actions
solution.explanation: Students open an account, deposit small amounts every month and watch interest make the balance grow. Only regular deposits make the balance grow.
steps: Result in the sentence: the balance grows
Monthly action that makes a balance grow: depositing
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Withdraw' and 'waste' would shrink the balance. Students do not 'lend' amounts into their own savings account.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: positive outcome signalled by the context
solution.explanation: The sentence reports a good result: students become more careful about comparing prices and less likely to buy on impulse. 'Careful' matches 'less likely to buy things on impulse'.
steps: The second half of the sentence is positive: less impulse buying
The first half must also be positive
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Careless' contradicts the positive result. 'Famous' and 'angry' make no sense with 'about comparing prices'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: contrast marked by 'need not be ... ; it can be as ordinary as...'
solution.explanation: The sentence contrasts what talking about money is feared to be with what it can be: ordinary. The contrasting word is 'awkward'.
steps: Structure: 'need not be X; it can be as ordinary as...'
X must be the opposite of ordinary and easy
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Routine', 'common' and 'casual' all mean much the same as 'ordinary', so they destroy the contrast.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (6). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: grammar ('be + better + past participle + to')
solution.explanation: 'Is far better equipped to make decisions' uses the past participle 'equipped' after 'is ... better'. It means better prepared.
steps: A past participle used as an adjective is needed: equipped
'is far better equipped to make' is correct
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Equip' (base form) and 'equipping' (present participle) do not fit after 'is better'. 'Equipment' is a noun.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: contrast with 'but' and the sentence that follows
solution.explanation: The battery is unfit for driving, 'but that does not mean it is useless': the next sentence says it can still store a great deal of energy and be given a second life.
steps: 'but that does not mean it is ___' denies a negative conclusion
The next sentence shows the battery still has a use
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Valuable' would make the sentence say the battery is not valuable, contradicting the next sentence. 'Charged' and 'expensive' do not follow from being unfit for driving.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: collocation ('dependence on imports')
solution.explanation: The metals are concentrated in a handful of countries, so recovering them reduces costs and the country's dependence on imports. 'Dependence on' is the fixed collocation.
steps: Context: metals come from a few countries, i.e. through imports
Recycling reduces the need to import
'dependence on imports' fits in meaning and preposition
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Emphasis on imports', 'insistence on imports' and 'interest on imports' make no sense here: recycling metals does not reduce any of them.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: action that explains the pollution that follows
solution.explanation: Informal dealers take the valuable parts and dump the rest, 'often in ways that pollute soil and water'. Only dumping explains the pollution.
steps: The phrase after the blank: 'in ways that pollute soil and water'
What would dealers do with parts they do not want? Throw them away
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Preserve', 'polish' and 'insure' are careful handling, which cannot pollute soil and water.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: contrast 'not a waste problem but a ___'
solution.explanation: The sentence contrasts a waste problem with something positive: a source of raw material for new vehicles.
steps: Structure: 'not X but Y' where X is negative
Y must be positive and fit 'of raw material'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Shortage' and 'lack' of raw material would be problems, not the positive opposite. 'Burden' repeats the idea of a problem.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: group lending and the phrasal verb 'vouch for'
solution.explanation: In group lending, members guarantee each other's repayment. 'Vouch for' means to guarantee or answer for someone, which explains why such borrowers are reliable.
steps: The sentence lists conditions that make borrowers reliable
Group members standing guarantee for each other is one such condition
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Argue for' and 'compete for' one another do not make borrowers more reliable. 'Apologise for one another' is illogical here.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: what income does to debt ('support' = sustain, service)
solution.explanation: Total debt grew 'well beyond what its income could support', i.e. beyond the level the household's income could service. The next sentence (repayments stopped) confirms the overload.
steps: The subject is 'its income'; the object is the debt
Income either can or cannot sustain a level of debt
solution.why_others_wrong: Income does not 'earn', 'waste' or 'spend' debt; with 'income' as subject these verbs make no sense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: purpose of a regulation
solution.explanation: Credit bureaus and repayment limits are meant to restrain over-lending, which had caused distress. 'Curb' means to restrain or control.
steps: The rules respond to over-lending that caused distress
Their aim must be to restrain it
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Encourage' and 'reward' over-lending contradict the purpose of the rules. 'Ignore' makes the rules pointless.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: concluding generalisation drawn from the paragraph
solution.explanation: The paragraph says an institution that rewards volume 'will always find ways around a ceiling', whatever the rules intend. The generalisation is that incentives override intentions: what people are rewarded for wins over what they mean to do.
steps: Paragraph point: good rules are defeated by bad incentives
The last sentence generalises: incentives beat intentions
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Follow', 'obey' and 'reflect' make incentives subordinate to, or consistent with, intentions, which reverses the paragraph's point.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (1) may be wrongly used. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the bold word must fit the logic of the sentence
solution.explanation: The sentence says heat builds up because the trees and soil that would otherwise reduce it have been paved over. 'Aggravate' (make worse) reverses this; 'moderate' (make less extreme) is correct.
steps: Logic: paving over trees and soil makes the city hotter
So trees and soil must have reduced the heat
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Intensify' and 'trap' repeat the error of 'aggravate': they make trees the cause of heat. The original word is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (2) may be wrongly used. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: meaning plus the comparative form after 'make the problem'
solution.explanation: Air conditioners pump hot air into the streets, so they make the heat problem worse, not 'better'. After 'make the problem', the comparative adjective 'worse' is required.
steps: Effect of pumping hot air into streets: more heat
Comparative needed: 'worse' (not the superlative 'worst' or the adverb 'well')
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Worst' is a superlative and needs 'the' and a comparison set. 'Well' is an adverb/adjective that does not fit the meaning. 'Better' itself is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (3) may be wrongly used. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: a list of harmful consequences
solution.explanation: The sentence lists the harms of prolonged heat: illness, lower labour productivity and higher electricity demand. Heat 'reduces' productivity; 'elevates' wrongly makes it a benefit.
steps: The sentence opens 'The consequences are not merely uncomfortable': it lists harms
Heat lowers the output of workers
Replace 'elevates' with 'reduces' (same tense and number as 'raises' and 'pushes')
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Enhances' has the same wrong meaning as 'elevates'. 'Elevating' is both wrong in meaning and breaks the parallel verbs 'raises ... pushes'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (4) may be wrongly used. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: 'if least ...' concession is correct as written
solution.explanation: 'One of the most serious, if least visible, threats' means serious though not easily seen. Heat is invisible compared with floods or fires, so 'visible' is correct as written.
steps: 'If' here means 'though': serious though least visible
The meaning is sound, so no replacement is needed
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Least invisible' is a confusing double negative that would make heat an obvious threat, which is not the point. 'Visibly' is an adverb and 'visibility' a noun; neither can modify 'threats' here. Since 'visible' is already correct, no replacement is needed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (5) may be wrongly used. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the following sentences decide the word
solution.explanation: The next sentences say a tree needs several years of care and a roof must be repainted as it fades: cooling a city is 'a habit of maintenance'. That calls for 'sustained' attention, not 'occasional' attention.
steps: Read what follows: years of care, repainting, 'a habit of maintenance'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Sporadic' and 'momentary' mean the same kind of irregular or brief attention as 'occasional', so they keep the error. 'Occasional' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Each of the new trainees (A) / have been assigned (B) / to a rural branch this year. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: to a rural branch this year.

solution.concept: 'Each of + plural noun' takes a singular verb
solution.explanation: 'Each' is the subject, and it is singular; 'of the new trainees' only describes it. So the verb must be 'has been assigned', not 'have been assigned'.
steps: 'Each' is singular, so the verb must be singular
'have been assigned' → 'has been assigned': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject phrase and part C is a correct adverbial phrase. Since B has an error, 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
He did not knew (A) / that the branch (B) / would remain closed on Saturday. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: After the auxiliary 'did', the main verb takes the base form
solution.explanation: 'Did not' must be followed by the base form of the verb: 'did not know', not 'did not knew'.
steps: Locate the auxiliary 'did' in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct 'that' clause opener, and 'would remain' in part C correctly follows the past reporting verb. Part A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: He did not knew

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The cashier counted the notes (A) / carefully before (B) / handing them over to the customer. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: handing them over to the customer.

solution.concept: Checking each part: verb form, adverb placement, gerund after a preposition
solution.explanation: The sentence is correct. 'Counted' is a correct past tense, 'carefully' correctly modifies 'counted', and 'before' (a preposition here) is correctly followed by the gerund 'handing'.
steps: Part A: subject + past tense + object: correct
Part C: 'before handing them over': preposition + gerund, correct
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of parts A, B and C is grammatically correct, as shown in the steps, so none of them is the answer.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
She has been working (A) / in this bank (B) / since five years. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Since' takes a point of time; 'for' takes a period of time
solution.explanation: 'Five years' is a period, so it needs 'for': 'for five years'. 'Since' is used with a point in time, such as 'since 2021'.
steps: Part C has a time expression: 'five years'
It is a period, not a starting point
'since five years' → 'for five years': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Has been working' (part A) is the correct present perfect continuous with a duration, and part B is correct. Part C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
One of my friend (A) / has opened a savings account (B) / in a public sector bank. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'One of' is followed by a plural noun
solution.explanation: 'One of' picks one member of a group, so the noun after it must be plural: 'one of my friends'.
steps: Locate 'One of my friend' in part A
Rule: one of + plural noun (+ singular verb)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Has opened' in part B correctly agrees with the singular subject 'One'. Part C is correct. Part A has the error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: One of my friend

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The committee has submitted (A) / its report, which recommend (B) / stricter norms for digital lenders. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: In a relative clause, the verb agrees with the antecedent of 'which'
solution.explanation: 'Which' refers to 'its report', which is singular. So the verb must be 'recommends', not 'recommend'.
steps: The verb in the relative clause must agree with it: 'recommends'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is correct: 'committee' acting as one body takes 'has' and 'its'. Part C is correct. Part B has the error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: its report, which recommend

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
No sooner had the auditors (A) / arrived at the branch (B) / when the manager produced the ledgers. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: when the manager produced the ledgers.

solution.concept: 'No sooner' pairs with 'than', not 'when'
solution.explanation: The correlative is 'No sooner ... than'. Part C uses 'when', which belongs with 'hardly' or 'scarcely'. It should read 'than the manager produced the ledgers'.
steps: Part A starts with 'No sooner had ...' (correct inversion)
'when' in part C → 'than': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A has the correct inversion 'No sooner had the auditors' and part B the correct past participle. Part C has the error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: when the manager produced the ledgers.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The number of customers using (A) / mobile banking apps have (B) / risen sharply over the last year. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: risen sharply over the last year.

solution.concept: 'The number of' takes a singular verb; 'a number of' takes a plural verb
solution.explanation: The subject is 'The number', a single quantity, so the verb must be 'has risen', not 'have risen'.
steps: 'of customers using mobile banking apps' only describes it
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject phrase. Part C, 'risen sharply', is correct with 'has'. Part B has the error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: mobile banking apps have

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Unless the borrower does not repay (A) / the overdue amount by Friday, (B) / the bank will initiate recovery proceedings. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Unless the borrower does not repay
the bank will initiate recovery proceedings.

solution.concept: 'Unless' already means 'if not'; it is not followed by another 'not'
solution.explanation: 'Unless the borrower does not repay' is a double negative meaning 'if the borrower does not not repay'. It should be 'Unless the borrower repays' (or 'If the borrower does not repay').
steps: Adding 'does not' creates a double negative and reverses the meaning
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is correct, and part C correctly uses the future in the main clause of a first conditional. Part A has the error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Unless the borrower does not repay

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The new policy, along with its detailed guidelines, (A) / has been published (B) / on the bank's official website. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The new policy, along with its detailed guidelines,

solution.concept: 'Along with', 'as well as', 'together with' do not change the number of the subject
solution.explanation: The subject is 'The new policy' (singular); 'along with its detailed guidelines' is a parenthetical addition. So the singular 'has been published' is correct, and 'published on the website' is idiomatic. The sentence has no error.
steps: 'on the bank's official website' is correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A student who counts the guidelines as part of the subject may wrongly pick part B; parts A and C are also correct, so only 'No error' fits.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Neither of the two proposals (A) / submitted by the consultants (B) / were acceptable to the board. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Neither of + plural noun' takes a singular verb
solution.explanation: 'Neither' (not one of the two) is the subject and is singular. The verb must be 'was acceptable', not 'were'.
steps: 'of the two proposals submitted by the consultants' describes it
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is the correct form 'Neither of the two' and part B is a correct participle phrase. Part C has the error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: were acceptable to the board.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Scarcely a week passes (A) / without some new scheme being announced (B) / for farmers who's crops have failed. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: without some new scheme being announced
for farmers who's crops have failed.

solution.concept: 'Whose' (possessive relative) vs 'who's' (who is / who has)
solution.explanation: The relative pronoun must show possession: the crops belong to the farmers. 'Who's' means 'who is' or 'who has', so it should be 'whose crops have failed'.
steps: Test 'who's' by expanding it: 'who is crops' / 'who has crops' make no sense
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A ('Scarcely a week passes') and part B ('without ... being announced') are correct idioms. Part C has the error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: for farmers who's crops have failed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The chairman, as well as the directors, (A) / were present at the meeting (B) / where the merger was finally approved. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The chairman, as well as the directors,
where the merger was finally approved.

solution.concept: With 'as well as', the verb agrees with the first subject
solution.explanation: The subject is 'The chairman' (singular); 'as well as the directors' is parenthetical. The verb must be 'was present', not 'were'.
steps: 'as well as the directors' does not make it plural
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is correctly punctuated with commas around the parenthetical phrase, and part C is correct. Part B has the error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: were present at the meeting

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
It is high time the government takes (A) / concrete steps to curb (B) / the misuse of farm loan waivers. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: It is high time the government takes
the misuse of farm loan waivers.

solution.concept: 'It is high time' + subject + past (subjunctive) form
solution.explanation: 'It is (high) time' is followed by the simple past to show that the action is overdue: 'It is high time the government took concrete steps'.
steps: Identify the structure 'It is high time + clause'
Rule: the verb in the clause takes the past form
solution.why_others_wrong: Parts B and C ('concrete steps to curb the misuse of ...') are correct. Part A has the error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: It is high time the government takes

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Not only did the bank reduce its lending rate, (A) / but it also waived (B) / the processing fee for first-time borrowers. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Not only did the bank reduce its lending rate,
the processing fee for first-time borrowers.

solution.concept: 'Not only' at the start needs inversion; it pairs with 'but ... also'
solution.explanation: The sentence is correct. 'Not only' at the start correctly triggers inversion ('did the bank reduce'), and the second clause correctly uses 'but it also waived'. The fee phrase is correct.
steps: Part A: 'Not only did the bank reduce' = auxiliary + subject + base verb: correct
Part B: 'but it also waived' = correct partner of 'not only'
solution.why_others_wrong: Students often expect 'not only' to need 'but also' together and mark part B, but 'but it also' is standard. Part A's inversion is required, not an error. Part C is correct.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The reason he was denied the loan (A) / was because his credit score (B) / had fallen below the bank's cut-off. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The reason he was denied the loan
had fallen below the bank's cut-off.

solution.concept: 'The reason ... is/was that', not 'is/was because' (redundancy)
solution.explanation: 'Reason' already means cause, so 'the reason ... was because' says the cause twice. The standard form is 'The reason he was denied the loan was that his credit score had fallen...'.
steps: Subject 'The reason ...' + 'was' needs a noun clause as complement
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is correct (the relative 'that/why' may be omitted after 'reason'). Part C correctly uses the past perfect for the earlier event. Part B has the error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: was because his credit score

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The bank **has opened two new branches last month** in the district.

options.text: opened two new branches last month
had opened two new branches last month
has been opening two new branches last month

solution.concept: Present perfect is not used with a finished past time ('last month')
solution.explanation: 'Last month' is a definite past time, so the simple past is required: 'The bank opened two new branches last month'.
steps: Spot the time marker: 'last month' (finished past)
Present perfect cannot take a finished past time marker
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Had opened' (past perfect) needs another past action to precede. 'Has been opening' is still a present perfect form and clashes with 'last month'. The original is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.
solution.final_answer: Option A: opened two new branches last month

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
He is **senior than** me by three years in the bank.

solution.concept: Latin comparatives (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior) take 'to', not 'than'
solution.explanation: 'Senior' is a Latin comparative and is followed by 'to': 'He is senior to me by three years'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Seniors' is a plural noun and cannot follow 'He is' here. 'Senior from' is not idiomatic. The original 'senior than' is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The loan was sanctioned **despite of his poor credit history**.

options.text: in spite his poor credit history
despite to his poor credit history

solution.concept: 'Despite' takes no preposition; 'in spite' needs 'of'
solution.explanation: 'Despite' is itself a preposition and is followed directly by a noun phrase: 'despite his poor credit history'. The alternative is 'in spite of'.
steps: 'Despite of' is a mixing of 'despite' and 'in spite of'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'In spite his' drops the necessary 'of'. 'Despite to' adds a wrong preposition. The original is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.
solution.final_answer: Option C: despite his poor credit history

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**Having finished the audit, the report was submitted** to the head office on Monday.

options.text: Having finished the audit, the team submitted the report
Having been finished the audit, the report was submitted
Having finished the audit, the report has submitted
